1:
The opening summons is read as a legal one. Henry makes the figure explicit: the scope of these verses is to convince the people that God has a controversy with them, and they are called to hear it as a prisoner at the bar is told to hearken to his indictment, that they may consider what answer to make. They would not regard the counsel often spoken to them, and now must hear the reproof, for God will act as he has spoken. Gill reads the imperative pastorally: they are to receive it as the word of God and not of men, apply it to themselves as those to whom it justly belongs, and improve it by humiliation and reformation. Calvin explains why the formula was needed. The prophet saw his doctrine held in contempt, and probably repeated these words often; the pride of that people had to be beaten down, and by bringing forward the divine name he shows they have not to do with a mortal man, or with a shepherd such as he was.

Keil and Delitzsch use the same formula to settle the shape of the book. The repeated call to hear, opening three successive chapters, suggests three addresses, but the contents show they are not separate sermons; they group the leading thoughts of spoken appeals into one long admonition to repentance, beginning with the proofs of the prophet's right to predict judgment, then exposing Israel's wickedness, then the worthlessness of its trust in idolatry, and lastly announcing the kingdom's destruction. Clarke outlines this chapter alone and praises the manner: the image the prophet uses, borrowed from his former calling, is natural and significant and not a little dignified by his lofty air.

Who is addressed is disputed on a phrase. Ellicott notes that children of Israel is not the usual expression here, so many manuscripts substitute house of Israel, but finds significance in the received reading, since the prophet addresses both kingdoms in speaking of the whole family, though the northern seems chiefly in his mind. Clarke divides the chapter so too, the twelve tribes reproved at the opening and the northern kingdom afterwards. Henry insists on the wider reference too: not the ten tribes only but Judah must take notice, since it is spoken against the whole family brought up out of Egypt.

The clause about being known produces the real division, and it turns on what therefore means. Gill takes the knowing as distinguishing love rather than bare omniscience, since all families are known to God but none with this affection or distinguished by these favours, temporal and spiritual alike, the land and the law and the worship. Clarke reads it as election and makes the inference proportional: the punishment shall answer to the privileges enjoyed and the grace abused. Wesley says the same in a line, chosen as peculiar ones and therefore judged for abusing these mercies. Ellicott begins in the same place, that the knowledge of God is love and on such knowledge followed privileges innumerable, but declines the proportional reading. It may mean the doom answers to the privileges, he allows, but more probably the intimacy is the ground of gracious chastisement, since to be allowed to go on in sin without rebuke is the greatest curse that can befall a nation or a man. Calvin rejects a different reading. Many think the prophet is conceding what the Israelites boasted of, that they were separated from the common class of men by adoption; but it seems rather a reproach, God bringing forward his benefits to enhance the sin of a people returning the worst recompense to one who had treated them so kindly. Keil and Delitzsch note what the claim provoked: the proud and self-secure would not hear such prophesying, which is why the chain of similes follows.
3:
The chain of questions is understood as an argument for the prophet's credentials, and Calvin sets out its structure. He reduces the similitudes to five particulars: that the prophet utters no empty words but has God's authority; that God announces punishment beforehand so men may repent, and does not cry out for no reason as unreflecting men grow angry for nothing; and that nothing happens by chance. Clarke reaches the same conclusion: no calamity falls on any people but by the express will of God on account of their iniquities, and whatever the prophets foretold they had by direct revelation.

Who the two walkers are is the first real dispute, and Ellicott canvasses it. Some say two prophets; one scholar says God and the prophet; but four others, whom he follows with more reason, refer it to God and Israel, since obedience and communion of heart are what scripture calls walking with God. The question is whether God will walk with man, guiding and shielding him, if man is not in harmony with him; and this is the first of a series of sayings all requiring a negative answer. Gill works the plain picture first: two cannot walk together without appointing time and place and road, nor amicably unless united in affection, or they fall out by the way; without friendship there is no fellowship and without concord no communion. Clarke turns it into direct address in the divine person: while you loved and served me I walked among you, but now our natures are opposite, and I can hold communion with you no longer. Wesley puts it in one question.

The lion divides them over what the roar signifies. Gill takes the roar for prophecy itself, compared to it elsewhere, and holds it never comes in judgment without a cause, the cause being the sin that makes a nation a prey. He describes the animal precisely: it roars when it first sees the prey, terrifying it so it cannot move, and roars again over it to invite others to share. Calvin makes the argument against the scoffers, who supposed the air was only made to reverberate when the prophets threatened: if lions do not roar except when they have obtained a prey, shall God cry from heaven when there is none? Ellicott presses the tense rather than the cause: the questions suggest the prey is at this moment being seized, and he distinguishes the roar in the forest from the growl of the famished young in the den, one scholar making the second word a hunting lion rather than a beast in its lair. The threat signifies that the nations and this family are even now trembling in the grasp of the great Avenger. Clarke reduces it to a question: would he threaten such a judgment without cause?

The snare is where the readings part most widely. Gill takes it for providence, since a bird is never taken without a snare set by the fowler's design and God's will, so no affliction comes without appointment. Calvin adds why men miss it: calamity comes unexpectedly and is ascribed to chance, but nets do not weave themselves. Ellicott corrects the rendering instead, preferring does the snare rise up from the ground and take nothing at all, blaming the received take up on an ambiguity in the Hebrew; his application is concrete, that Israel like a silly dove is falling into snares which may be seen springing from the earth even now, the armies that will enclose her being already in motion. Clarke calls the passage curious and deserving further consideration, and reconstructs the mechanism, translating whether the trap shall arise from the ground and, catching, not catch; he finds an allusion to a spring trap of the kind used for vermin, whose jaws open backward and press on a spring held by a key.
6:
The trumpet is the last similitude, read as an argument from ordinary alarm. Gill is careful which trumpet is meant: not the silver trumpet that gathered the people to worship, nor the jubilee trumpet that proclaimed liberty, but the alarm of war blown by watchmen who have descried an enemy. Clarke says the same briefly, the sign of alarm and invasion, and asks whether a people would not provide for their defence. Calvin turns the comparison into a reproach for torpor. When a trumpet sounds all tremble and men either fly for aid or stand amazed; God himself cries, and his voice deserves far more attention than a trumpet that fills men's minds with dread, yet it is a sound uttered to the deaf. What does this prove, he asks, but that madness possesses their minds?

On the evil in the city the expositors are careful about the word. Clarke states the restriction plainly: it does not mean moral evil but punishment for sin, natural evil being the punishment of moral evil, which God sends when the latter is persisted in; and he asks whether any public calamity can befall the wicked that is not an effect of divine displeasure. Wesley glosses the noun as plague or famine and guards the verb: God does it by his own hand or by those he employs, and whoever the instruments, he is the principal agent. Gill takes the next verse as absolutely: nothing remarkable happens in the world or in a nation apart from him.

That the secret is revealed to the prophets is read as mercy and as distinction. Clarke says the prophets are in strict correspondence with God, who shows them things to come so they may inform the people, that by repentance the people may avoid the evil and by walking closely with God secure his favour. Calvin makes it a matter of comparative privilege. God did not deal with Israel as with the heathen: other peoples he punished without warning, summoning neither the Edomites nor the Ammonites nor the Egyptians to judgment but executing vengeance without addressing them. With Israel he not only recalled them by his scourges but preceded the scourges with his word, so every excuse was taken away.

The closing pair of questions returns to the lion, and the expositors divide over the second of them. Gill hears the prophet's own experience in the first, since as a herdsman in the wilderness he had often heard a lion roar and been put in a panic for himself and for his cattle. Wesley reads it as the roar of a beast near its prey, so God has terribly threatened what is near to be done, and takes the answering clause simply: the prophet cannot but speak what he has heard. Ellicott refers the imagery back to the opening of the book and to the lion of the earlier verse, and finds the voice of the Lord so clearly portending judgment that universal terror inevitably follows; he compares the saying that if these should hold their peace the stones would cry out. Clarke agrees on the first question and proposes a different sense for the second. The verb should be taken in what he calls its natural and ideal signification, to pray or deprecate vengeance, so the question becomes not who can help proclaiming the judgment but who can help supplicating mercy that it may be averted. Calvin reads the verse against the hearers, as a reproof of their habit of contending with the prophets when their sins were sharply reprehended. Men do not consider that prophets are sent from above with a charge; when the words are severe the world clamours and asks what these men intend, why they urge so much, why they will not let us rest, since they provoke God's wrath against us.
9:
The summons to the foreigners is a legal device, and Calvin names it outright. The prophet begins here to set judges over the Israelites, since they would not submit to God's judgment, and the judges are Egyptians and Edomites; God had cited them to his own tribunal while hope of reconciliation remained, and when they clamoured against his servants as though guilty of no fault, nothing else was left. Gill reads the errand more mildly: the prophets are to publish the sins and the threatened punishment in the courts of the Philistines and Egyptians, and let these heathen judge whether there was not a just proportion between them. Henry frames it as public notice to the neighbours, the summons going to a chief Philistine city and then to Egypt, so the great men of both nations, conversant with the public intelligence, may assemble on the mountains around the capital. Wesley says it in a line: strangers are invited to observe what cause there is for the threatening.

Two details of staging are corrected. Clarke observes that the flat housetops were where public declarations were made, and Ellicott presses the preposition to the same end: on the palaces rather than in them, that is, on their roofs, conspicuous enough for the population high and low to hear. He places the observers on the high ground from which everything passing in the metropolis can be watched, and would adopt the marginal rendering oppressions on the strength of the parallelism. Wesley glosses the two nouns as seditious counsels and multitudes of oppressed, since the usurpers took it for their interest to crush all they feared, and extends the scene to the whole kingdom.

That they know not to do right is where the best work is done, since none will let the phrase excuse anything. Gill takes it practically: they had used themselves so long to unjust ways that they had lost the practical knowledge of justice, knowing what was right in theory but not in practice; he refers it chiefly to judges whose eyes bribes had blinded. Clarke turns it into an epigram: those who do wrong to their own ruin must be ignorant of what is right, but none are so blind as those who will not see. Ellicott states it most severely. They have not merely lost the perception of what is right but are indifferent to it; they know not and care not, the awful state of moral impotence in which not the consciousness only but the impulses to action are paralysed, a dead conscience. Nothing is more condemnatory: the light within them is darkness. Calvin agrees that ignorance lessens nothing: they had cast away everything just and sinned without shame, so that they are brute animals void of judgment, and the charge is wilful blindness. Wesley reads the storing up as men lay up wealth in treasuries, condemning the innocent and seizing his substance.

On the adversary the identification is made cautiously by one and flatly by another. Ellicott prefers adversary to the affliction of two ancient versions, since it is the subject of the following verb, and takes the Assyrian to be meant though not named; he dismisses as incoherent the Greek reading, which addresses Tyre and confounds two similar words. Wesley names the Assyrian without hesitation and has him beset the whole land as one besieged city. Clarke puts it as a sentence: wherever they turn they shall meet a foe. Calvin rejects a grammatical proposal, that the noun is a verb in the imperative, and draws out why the encirclement matters: the ungodly always seek escapes and think they can get out through the smallest hole, and though disheartened when hemmed in, still seek subterfuges to right and left. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch connect the sentence to its cause, the tumults and robbery that ruin the kingdom.
12:
The shepherd and the lion give a figure all read alike and apply differently. Gill explains the practice: what is taken from the lion's mouth is what the beast has left, produced to the master as evidence that the sheep was torn, since it would be daring to take anything from a lion otherwise. Clarke draws the sense out plainly: scarcely any shall escape, and those that do with extreme difficulty, as a shepherd recovers of a whole sheep no more than two legs or a piece of an ear, enough to prove it was his; the survivors will be of as little worth as the fragments. Wesley adds two identifications: the couch belongs to the chief city of Syria, taken about the time the Assyrian wasted Israel, and the few who escape are the poor, pitied when the enemy finds them sick on their beds. Ellicott corrects the verb to delivereth and be delivered, following the margin, and takes the shanks and pieces of ear, worthless portions saved from the jaws, for the remnants that shall escape; on the clause about Damascus he calls the rival construction very questionable and prefers the reading of most Hebrew texts. Calvin warns against misreading the concession. That some would be saved does not mitigate the severity already announced, but shows that if any are saved it is not because the people defended themselves, but as when a trembling shepherd snatches a small portion from a lion's mouth.

Keil and Delitzsch read the fresh summons as a deliberate device, the threat brought into peculiar prominence by a new introduction. Who is addressed divides the rest. Gill takes it of the prophets and priests, whose business was to admonish the people of their danger, and Wesley agrees, glossing the divine title as Lord of all. Ellicott takes it quite differently, as addressed to the foreign nations summoned a few verses earlier.

On the altars they part over history and doctrine. Gill notes that the idolatry is named here though passed over in the appeal to the heathen princes, who were guilty of it themselves, and lists the transgressions visited: profaneness, luxury, and oppression of the poor. Clarke supplies a fulfilment from the annals: the reforming king who destroyed the idolatry, pulled down the altars consecrated to idol worship, and burnt the bones of the priests upon them. Calvin makes it a warning against false confidence: the superstitions they trusted in would lead them to ruin rather than help them. When they heard God was offended they looked on their sacrifices as a shield, which is how hypocrites mock God; but what was offered at that shrine was mere profanation.

The houses at the end are described with care, and one uncertainty admitted. Gill allows either two dwellings, a town house for warmth in winter and a country house for the air in summer, or two parlours in one house, and takes the threat to reach city and country alike; one commentator refers the shaking to the earthquake predicted elsewhere. Ellicott says outright that it is uncertain whether two classes of royal abode or different chambers of one house are meant, the parallels admitting either; he glosses the ivory houses as mansions adorned with ivory and would read many houses for great houses. Clarke takes the wider sense and adds a traveller's illustration: the hills around a certain North African city are beautified with country seats, little white houses to which the better sort retire during the heats. Wesley divides them so too, the winter house in the chief city and the summer houses as places of pleasure. Calvin reads the whole as a rebuke of confidence in wealth: abundance blinds men and they imagine themselves inaccessible in great palaces, so the prophet declares these houses will be no impediment to God's vengeance, the poor being content with one cottage for both seasons.
